en: Thus have I heard: the Potaliya Sutta, the fifty-fourth discourse of the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Aṅguttarāpas at a town of theirs named Āpaṇa.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Āpaṇa for alms.
Having walked for alms in Āpaṇa, after his meal, returning from his almsround, he approached a certain grove for his midday rest.

Having entered that grove, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest. Meanwhile, the householder Potaliya—well-dressed in lower and upper garments, carrying a sunshade and sandals—was walking and wandering about on foot for exercise when he approached that grove; having approached and entered that grove, he went to where the Venerable Sāriputta was. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta and, having concluded his polite conversation, stood to one side. Standing there, the householder Potaliya said this to the Venerable Sāriputta: “Venerable Sāriputta, it is wonderful, truly wonderful! How well-spoken were these words: ‘One who does not see things as they really are, does not know suffering as it really is; one who does not see things as they really are, does not know the origin of suffering as it really is; one who does not see things as they really are, does not know the cessation of suffering as it really is; one who does not see things as they really are, does not know the way leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is. “Householder, it is because one sees things as they really are that one knows suffering as it really is; it is because one sees things as they really are that one knows the origin of suffering as it really is; it is because one sees things as they really are that one knows the cessation of suffering as it really is; it is because one sees things as they really are that one knows the way leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is. “But, Venerable Sāriputta, how is it that by seeing things as they really are, one knows suffering as it really is? How is it that by seeing things as they really are, one knows the origin of suffering as it really is? How is it that by seeing things as they really are, one knows the cessation of suffering as it really is? How is it that by seeing things as they really are, one knows the way leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is? “Householder, it is by seeing form as it really is—with its origin, its passing away, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it—that one knows form as it really is. It is by seeing feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as it really is—with its origin, its passing away, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it—that one knows consciousness as it really is. It is in this way, householder, that by seeing things as they really are, one knows suffering as it really is; it is in this way that by seeing things as they really are, one knows the origin of suffering as it really is; it is in this way that by seeing things as they really are, one knows the cessation of suffering as it really is; it is in this way that by seeing things as they really are, one knows the way leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is. “Venerable Sāriputta, it is wonderful, truly wonderful! How well-spoken were these words: ‘It is by seeing form as it really is—with its origin, its passing away, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it—that one knows form as it really is... It is by seeing consciousness as it really is—with its origin, its passing away, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it—that one knows consciousness as it really is. “Householder, what do you think? Is form permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, venerable sir. “But is what is impermanent suffering or happiness? “Suffering, venerable sir. “But is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “No, venerable sir. “Is feeling permanent or impermanent?... Is perception permanent or impermanent?... Are volitional formations permanent or impermanent?... Is consciousness permanent or impermanent? “Impermanent, venerable sir. “But is what is impermanent suffering or happiness? “Suffering, venerable sir. “But is it fitting to regard what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’? “No, venerable sir. “Therefore, householder, whatever form has been, will be, or is now present—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all that form should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Whatever feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness has been, will be, or is now present—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all that consciousness should be seen as it really is with correct wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self. Seeing this thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one becomes disenchanted with form, disenchanted with feeling, disenchanted with perception, disenchanted with volitional formations, and disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, one is liberated. Through liberation, there is the knowledge: ‘It is liberated. One understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more coming to any state of being. “Venerable Sāriputta, it is wonderful, truly wonderful! Just as if one were to turn upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to carry an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Venerable Sāriputta in many ways. I go to the Venerable Sāriputta for refuge and to the Dhamma and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. From this day forth, may the Venerable Sāriputta accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life. Then the householder Potaliya, having approached the Venerable Sāriputta, paid homage to him and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dhamma. Then the householder Potaliya, having been instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened by the Venerable Sāriputta with a discourse on the Dhamma, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Venerable Sāriputta, and keeping him on his right, departed. Then the householder Potaliya, having entered that grove, sat down at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest. The householder Potaliya, too, well-dressed in lower and upper garments, carrying a sunshade and sandals, was walking and wandering about on foot for exercise when he approached that grove; having approached and entered that grove, he went to where the Venerable Sāriputta was. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta and, having concluded his polite conversation, stood to one side. Standing there, the householder Potaliya said this to the Venerable Sāriputta: “Venerable Sāriputta, it is wonderful, truly wonderful! How well-spoken were these words: ‘One who does not see things as they really are, does not know suffering as it really is; one who does not see things as they really are, does not know the origin of suffering as it really is; one who does not see things as they really are, does not know the cessation of suffering as it really is; one who does not see things as they really are, does not know the way leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is. “Householder, it is because one sees things as they really are that one knows suffering as it really is; it is because one sees things as they really are that one knows the origin of suffering as it really is; it is because one sees things as they really are that one knows the cessation of suffering as it really is; it is because one sees things as they really are that one knows the way leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is. “But, Venerable Sāriputta, how is it that by seeing things as they really are, one knows suffering as it really is? How is it that by seeing things as they really are, one knows the origin of suffering as it really is? How is it that by seeing things as they really are, one knows the cessation of suffering as it really is? How is it that by seeing things as they really are, one knows the way leading to the cessation of suffering as it really is? “Householder, it is by seeing form as it really is—with its origin, its passing away, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it—that one knows form as it really is. It is by seeing feeling... perception... volitional formations... consciousness as it really is—with its origin, its passing away, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from
He approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he stood to one side. As Potaliya the householder was standing there, the Blessed One said to him:
"Householder, there are seats available; if you wish, sit down."
When this was said, the householder Potaliya, thinking, "The ascetic Gotama addresses me with the title 'householder,'" became angry and displeased and remained silent.
A second time, the Blessed One...
[as before] ...and a third time, the Blessed One said this to the householder Potaliya:
“There are seats available, householder; if you wish, please sit down.
When this was said, the householder Potaliya thought, “The ascetic Gotama addresses me by the title ‘householder,’” and being angry and displeased, he said this to the Blessed One:
“This is improper, Master Gotama; this is unbecoming, that you address me by the title ‘householder.’”
“Householder, those are indeed your ways, those are your signs, those are your marks, as befits a householder.
“But it is because, Master Gotama, all my business activities have been abandoned and all my worldly dealings have been cut off.
“But how, householder, have all your business activities been abandoned and all your worldly dealings cut off?”
“Master Gotama, whatever wealth, grain, silver, or gold I once had has all been handed over as an inheritance to my sons. Therein, I live without reproach or blame, intent only on food and clothing.
Thus, Master Gotama, all my business affairs have been abandoned and all my worldly dealings have been cut off.
“But, householder, you speak of the cutting off of worldly dealings in one way, whereas in the discipline of the Noble One, the cutting off of worldly dealings occurs in another way.”
“But how, venerable sir, does the cutting off of worldly discourse occur in the Noble One’s Discipline?
It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma as to how the cutting off of worldly discourse occurs in the Noble One’s Discipline.
“In that case, householder, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the householder Potaliya replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Householder, these eight things lead to the cutting off of worldly discourse in the discipline of the Noble One.”
Which eight?
Based on abstaining from taking life, taking life is to be abandoned;
based on taking what is given, taking what is not given is to be abandoned.
Relying on truthful speech, false speech should be abandoned;
relying on non-divisive speech, divisive speech should be abandoned;
relying on freedom from greed and lust, greed and lust should be abandoned.
Dependent on blamelessness and non-resentment, blame and resentment are to be abandoned;
dependent on non-anger and non-distress, anger and distress are to be abandoned;
dependent on non-conceit, conceit is to be abandoned.
“Householder, these eight things have been stated by me in brief, not analyzed in detail; they lead to the cutting off of worldly discourse in the discipline of the Noble One.

“Venerable sir, as for these eight things that have been stated by the Blessed One in brief, not analyzed in detail, which lead to the cutting off of worldly discourse in the discipline of the Noble One—it would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One were to [explain] these eight things to me.”
“Please analyze this in detail out of compassion.
“In that case, householder, listen and pay close attention; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” the householder Potaliya replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“It was said: ‘Dependent upon abstention from taking life, taking life is to be abandoned. On what account was this said?
Here, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus:”
‘I am practicing for the abandoning and total eradication of those fetters on account of which I would be a killer of living beings.
If I were a killer of living beings, my own self would reproach me for that reason; wise people, having investigated, would also censure me for that reason;
and after the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination is to be expected for me on account of that killing.’
‘Indeed, this very thing is a fetter and this is an obstruction, namely, the taking of life.
And those taints, vexations, and fevers that might arise conditioned by the taking of life do not exist for one who abstains from taking life.
‘By relying on non-killing, the taking of life is to be abandoned’—thus it was said.
Thus it was said; this is said with reference to this.
“Depending on taking what is given, taking what is not given should be abandoned”—thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
Here, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus:
‘I am practicing for the abandoning and total eradication of those fetters because of which I would be a taker of what is not given.

If I were a taker of what is not given, others might censure me on account of that taking of what is not given; the wise, having investigated, might also reproach me on account of that taking of what is not given;
and upon the breakup of the body, after death, a miserable destination might be expected for me on account of that taking of what is not given.’
“Indeed, this very thing is a fetter and an obstruction, namely, taking what is not given.
And whatever taints, vexations, and fevers might arise conditioned by taking what is not given—those taints, vexations, and fevers do not exist for one who abstains from taking what is not given.
“By relying on taking what is given, taking what is not given is to be abandoned.”
Thus it was said; this is said with reference to this.
“Relying on truthful speech, false speech should be abandoned”—thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
Here, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus:
‘I am practicing for the abandoning and total eradication of those fetters on account of which I might be a liar.
If I were to be a liar, others would reproach me for that reason; the wise, having investigated, would also censure me for that reason;
and after the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination could be expected for me on account of that lying.’
“Indeed, this very thing is a fetter and an obscuration, namely, false speech.
And whatever taints, vexations, and fevers might arise on account of false speech—for one who abstains from false speech, those taints, vexations, and fevers do not exist.
“By relying on truthful speech, false speech is to be abandoned.”
Thus it was said; this is said with reference to this.
“Depending on non-slanderous speech, slanderous speech should be abandoned”—thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
Here, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus:
‘I am practicing for the abandoning and total eradication of those fetters on account of which I might be a speaker of divisive speech.
If I were to be a speaker of divisive speech, others would reproach me for that reason; the wise, having investigated, would also censure me for that reason;
and upon the breakup of the body, after death, a miserable destination is to be expected for me on account of that divisive speech.’
Moreover, this itself is a fetter and this is a hindrance, namely, malicious speech.
And those taints, vexations, and fevers that might arise conditioned by malicious speech do not exist for one who abstains from malicious speech.
“By relying on non-malicious speech, malicious speech is to be abandoned.”
Thus it was said; this is said with reference to this.
“By relying on non-greed and non-lust, greed and lust should be abandoned”—thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
Here, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus:
‘I am practicing for the abandoning and eradication of those fetters on account of which I might be greedy and covetous.
If I were to be greedy and covetous, others would reproach me for that greed and covetousness; the wise, having investigated, would also censure me for that greed and covetousness;
and upon the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination could be expected for me on account of that greed and covetousness.’
This very thing is the fetter, this is the hindrance, namely, greed and lust.
And whatever taints, vexations, and fevers might arise conditioned by greed and lust, these taints, vexations, and fevers do not exist for one who abstains from greed and lust.
“By relying on non-greed and non-lust, greed and lust are to be abandoned”—thus it was said.
Thus it was said; this was said with reference to this.
“Depending on blamelessness, blame is to be abandoned”—thus it was said. But with reference to what was this said?
Here, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus:
‘I am practicing for the abandoning and total eradication of those fetters on account of which I might be subject to blame.
If I were subject to blame, then because of that blame I would reproach myself; the wise, having investigated me, would also censure me because of that blame;
and upon the breakup of the body, after death, a miserable destination is to be expected because of that blame.’
Moreover, this very thing is a fetter and an hindrance, namely, resentment toward blame.
And whatever taints, vexations, and fevers might arise conditioned by resentment toward blame—those taints, vexations, and fevers do not exist for one who is without resentment toward blame.
“By relying on freedom from resentment toward blame, resentment toward blame is to be abandoned.”
Thus it was said; this is said with reference to this:
“Depending on freedom from anger and distress, anger and distress are to be abandoned. Thus it was said; with reference to what was this said?
Here, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus:
‘I am practicing for the abandoning and total eradication of those fetters on account of which I would become angry and distressed.
If I were to become angry and distressed, others might censure me for that anger and distress; the wise, having investigated, might also reproach me for that anger and distress;
and upon the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination might be expected for me on account of that anger and distress.’
This indeed is the fetter, this is the hindrance, namely, anger and resentment.
And whatever taints, vexations, and fevers might arise conditioned by anger and resentment, they do not exist for one who is without anger and resentment.
"By relying on freedom from anger and resentment, anger and resentment are to be abandoned"—thus it was said.
Thus it was said; this was said with reference to this.
“By relying on non-conceit, conceit should be abandoned”—thus it was said. With reference to what was this said?
Here, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus:
‘Those fetters on account of which I might be conceited—I am practicing for their abandoning and their total eradication.

If I were to be conceited, my own self would reproach me on account of that conceit; the wise, having investigated, would also censure me on account of that conceit; and after the breakup of the body, after death, a bad destination is to be expected on account of that conceit.
Indeed, this very conceit is itself a fetter and an obstruction.’
"And those taints, vexations, and fevers that might arise on account of conceit do not exist for one who is without conceit.
"By relying on non-conceit, conceit is to be abandoned"—
this is what was said, and it is in reference to this that it was said.
“These eight things, householder, have been spoken of in brief and analyzed in detail as those which lead to the cutting off of worldly discourse in the Noble One’s discipline;
yet, even so, there is not yet a complete cutting off of worldly discourse in every way and in all respects within the Noble One’s discipline.
“But how, venerable sir, does the complete cutting off of worldly discourse occur in every way and in all respects within the Noble One’s discipline?”

“It would be well for me, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in such a way that, according to the discipline of the Noble Ones, there is a total and complete cutting off of worldly discourse in every respect.
“In that case, householder, listen and attend closely; I shall speak.
“Yes, venerable sir,” the householder Potaliya replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
1. Discourse on the Danger of Sensual Pleasures:
“Householder, suppose there were a dog, overcome by hunger and weakness, standing before the slaughterhouse of a cow-killer.”
Suppose a skilled butcher or his apprentice were to throw down a skeleton of a cow— well-boned, stripped of flesh,
and smeared with blood. What do you think,
householder, would that dog, by gnawing at that skeleton— well-boned, stripped of flesh, and smeared with blood— be able to overcome its hunger and weakness?”
“No, venerable sir.
“For what reason?
“Because that skeleton, venerable sir, has been well-pulverized, thoroughly pulverized, boneless, yet smeared with blood.”
"But only so that the dog would partake in exhaustion and distress.
"In the same way, householder, the noble disciple reflects thus:
'Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to a skeleton; they bring much suffering and much despair; the danger therein is even greater.'"
Having seen this as it really is with correct wisdom, one avoids that equanimity which is diversified and based on diversity,
and develops instead that equanimity which is unified and based on unity, wherein the clinging to worldly material things ceases without remainder.
"Householder, it is just as if a vulture, a falcon, or a hawk were to seize a piece of meat and fly up with it.
Then other vultures, falcons, and hawks would pursue it again and again, tearing at it and snatching it away.
What do you think, householder?"
“If that vulture, or hawk, or falcon were not to quickly let go of that piece of meat, would it, on account of that, meet death or experience suffering amounting to death?”—
“Yes, venerable sir.”— “In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus:”
‘Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to a lump of meat; they bring much suffering and much despair, and the danger therein is even greater.

Having seen this as it really is with correct wisdom, one avoids that equanimity which is diversified and based on diversity, and instead cultivates that equanimity which is unified and based on unity, wherein the clinging to worldly material things ceases without remainder.
He develops that very equanimity.
Householder, it is just as if a man were to take a burning torch and walk against the wind.
What do you think, householder?
If that man did not quickly let go of that burning grass torch,
would it not burn his hand, or burn his arm, or burn some other limb or member of his body,
and because of that, would he not meet with death or suffering amounting to death?”
“Yes, venerable sir.
“In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus:
‘Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to a grass torch—full of suffering, full of despair; the danger here is even greater.’”
Having seen this thus as it really is with correct wisdom, one develops that very equanimity... Just as if, householder,
there were a charcoal pit deeper than a man’s height, full of glowing coals, smokeless and fireless,
and a person were to come along seeking life, not seeking death, desiring happiness and recoiling from suffering.
"Suppose two strong men were to seize him by both arms and drag him toward a pit of glowing embers.
What do you think, householder,
would that man twist his body this way and that?"
“Yes, venerable sir.
“And why is that? “Because, venerable sir, that man knows: ‘I shall fall into this charcoal pit, and because of that I will meet death or suffering as painful as death.’”
“In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus:
‘Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to a pit of glowing embers—full of suffering, full of despair; the danger here is even greater.
Having seen this as it really is with correct wisdom, ... [he] develops that very equanimity.”
"Just as, householder, a man might see in a dream delightful parks, delightful groves, delightful landscapes, and delightful lotus ponds,
yet upon waking he would not see anything at all;
even so, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus:"
“Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to a dream; they bring much suffering and much despair, and the danger therein is even greater.
… [as before] … he develops that very equanimity.
Householder, it is just as if a man, having requested borrowed wealth—such as a carriage fit for a nobleman or excellent jeweled earrings.
Thus, escorted and surrounded by those borrowed riches, he would enter the marketplace.
Seeing him, people would say:
"What a wealthy man indeed! Such are the riches that the wealthy enjoy!"
“Wherever the owners might see it, they would take it away from that very spot.
What do you think, householder, would that be sufficient cause for that man’s distress?
“Yes, venerable sir.”
“For what reason?
“Because, venerable sir, they take away what belongs to the owner.
“In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus:”
“Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to borrowed goods; they bring much suffering and much despair, and the danger therein is even greater.
… [as before] … he develops that very equanimity.
“Householder, suppose there were a dense forest thicket not far from a village or a town.”
In that place there was a tree endowed with fruit and laden with fruit, yet no fruits had fallen to the ground.
Then a man might come seeking fruit, searching for fruit, wandering in pursuit of fruit.
Having entered deep into that forest grove, he would see that tree, endowed with fruit and laden with fruit.
It might occur to him:
‘This tree is indeed abundant with fruit and well-laden with fruit, yet there are no fruits fallen upon the ground.
I know, however, how to climb this tree.’
‘What if I were to climb this tree, eat as much as I need, and fill my lap?
He would then climb that tree, eat as much as he needed, and fill his lap.
Then a second person would come along, seeking fruit, searching for fruit, wandering in search of fruit, carrying a sharp axe.
Having entered that forest grove, he would see that tree with its fruits both abundant and fully developed.
It would occur to him:
“This tree indeed has abundant and fully developed fruits, yet there are no fruits at all fallen upon the ground.”
‘But I do not know how to climb this tree.
Suppose I were to cut this tree down at its root, eat as much as I need, and fill my lap.
He would then cut that tree down right at its root.
"What do you think, householder?
Suppose that man who first climbed the tree were not to descend quickly;
as the tree fell, would it not break his hand, or break his foot, or break some other limb or another?"
“...he might break his limbs and joints, and because of that he would meet death or suffer pain amounting to death.
“Yes, venerable sir.
“In the same way, householder, a noble disciple reflects thus:”
“Sensual pleasures have been compared by the Blessed One to the fruit of a tree; they bring much suffering and much despair, and the danger therein is even greater.

Having seen this as it really is with correct wisdom, one should avoid that equanimity which is diversified and based on diversity, and instead cultivate that equanimity which is unified and based on unity, wherein the clinging to worldly material things ceases without remainder.
He develops that very equanimity.
Relying on this very supreme purity of mindfulness through equanimity, householder, that noble disciple recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say:
one birth, two births... [and so on] ...thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past lives.
"Householder, it is by relying on this very supreme purity of mindfulness through equanimity that a noble disciple,
with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, sees beings passing away and being reborn—
lowly and exalted, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate— and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma."
Indeed, householder, that noble disciple, by relying on this very supreme purity of mindfulness through equanimity,
having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom through the destruction of the taints,
dwells having attained it.
"To this extent, householder, in the discipline of the Noble One, there is a total and complete severance of worldly discourse in every way.
What do you think, householder:
since in the discipline of the Noble One there is a total and complete severance of worldly discourse in every way, do you perceive such a severance of worldly discourse within yourself?"
“And who, venerable sir, am I? And what is the total and complete cutting off of conventional expression in the Noble One’s Discipline?
I am far indeed, venerable sir, from the total and complete cutting off of conventional expression in the Noble One’s Discipline.

For formerly, venerable sir, though wanderers of other sects were actually not thoroughbreds, we thought they were thoroughbreds; though they were actually not thoroughbreds, we fed them the food of thoroughbreds; and though they were actually not thoroughbreds, we established them in the position of thoroughbreds.”

"But we, venerable sir, though being well-bred ourselves, thought of the monks as not well-bred; though being well-bred ourselves, we fed them the food of those who are not well-bred; though being well-bred ourselves, we placed them in the position of those who are not well-bred.
But now, venerable sir, though the wanderers of other sects are indeed not well-bred, we shall recognize them as such;

though they are indeed not well-bred, we shall feed them the food of those who are not well-bred; and though they are indeed not well-bred, we shall place them in the position of those who are not well-bred."

"But as for us, venerable sir, being thoroughbreds ourselves, we shall recognize them as thoroughbreds; being thoroughbreds ourselves, we shall feed them the food of thoroughbreds; being thoroughbreds ourselves, we shall establish them in the position of thoroughbreds.
Truly, venerable sir, the Blessed One has inspired in me love for recluses, confidence in recluses, and reverence for recluses among recluses.
Excellent, venerable sir! Excellent, venerable sir!"
"Just as, venerable sir, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost,
or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—
just so, venerable sir, has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways."
"Venerable sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.
The Potaliya Sutta, the fourth, is concluded.
